title: The rope of hair
translation: What people notice first about a woman is her hair. And you can tell what kind of person she is, and where she comes from, just from how she talks, even if you can't see her.
Even when she isn't trying, she can make a man lose his head. And women will go without sleep, wear themselves out, and put up with things nobody should have to put up with, all for love.
Desire runs deeper than anything. You can give up every other pleasure if you try. Not this one. Young or old, smart or stupid, nobody gets free of it.

That's why there's an old saying: a rope twisted from a woman's hair can hold even the biggest elephant, and a whistle made from a clog a woman has worn will always call the deer in autumn, when the stags are looking for mates. This is the one temptation you really need to watch yourself with.

{人|ひと}の{程|ほど}、{心|こころ}ばへなどは、{物|もの}うち{言|い}ひたるけはひにこそ、{物|もの}ごしにも{知|し}らるれ。

まことに{愛著|あいぢやく}の{道|みち}、その{根|ね}{深|ふか}く{源|みなもと}{遠|とほ}し。
{六|ろく}{塵|ぢん}の{楽欲|げうよく}{多|おほ}しといへども、{皆|みな}{厭離|おんり}しつべし。
その{中|なか}に、ただかの{惑|まど}ひのひとつ{止|や}めがたきのみぞ、{老|お}いたるも{若|わか}きも、{智|ち}あるも{愚|おろ}かなるも、{変|かは}る{所|ところ}なしとぞ{見|み}ゆる。
されば{女|をんな}の{髪筋|かみすぢ}を{縒|よ}れる{綱|つな}には、{大象|だいざう}もよくつながれ、{女|をんな}のはける{足駄|あしだ}にて{造|つく}れる{笛|ふえ}には、{秋|あき}の{鹿|しか}{必|かなら}ず{寄|よ}るとぞいひ{伝|つた}へ{侍|はべ}る。

literal: In a woman, it seems that splendid hair is surely what makes people notice her.
A person's standing, disposition and so on can be known from the impression of her speaking, even through a screen.

Even in her ordinary manner on any occasion she bewilders people's hearts; and in general, that women do not sleep at ease, do not think to spare themselves, and endure well even things that should be unbearable, is only because they think of love.
Truly, the way of attachment: its root is deep and its source distant.
Though the desires of the six senses are many, all of them can be renounced.
Among them, only that one bewilderment is hard to stop, and in it, old and young, wise and foolish, seem to be no different.

So it is handed down that with a rope twisted from strands of a woman's hair even a great elephant can be tied, and that to a flute made from a clog a woman has worn, the autumn deer will always come.
What one must admonish oneself about, fear and guard against, is this bewilderment.

notes.quote: 女は髪のめでたからむこそ
notes.text: In the Heian ideal, a noblewoman's hair was long, black and straight, often longer than she was tall. It was the first thing people praised.

{物|もの}ごし: 'through something', a screen or blind. Noblewomen usually spoke to men from behind a screen, so the voice and the way of speaking were often all a man had to go on. こそ … るれ: the realis form of る ('can be known').
{愛著|あいぢやく}: attachment, the Buddhist term for clinging to people and things. Modern {愛着|あいちやく} 'fondness, attachment' is the same word, without the warning.
The six 'dusts' ({塵|ぢん}): the objects of the six senses in Buddhism: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touch, and thoughts. {楽欲|げうよく}: desire for them. {厭離|おんり}: turning away from the world.
Both images are old sayings, and the elephant rope is usually traced to a Buddhist text. The deer flute works because in autumn the stags call for mates, and hunters used whistles to lure them.

notes.quote: ただ色を思ふがゆゑなり
notes.text: Before the warning, the text says that women are caught by love too: they go without sleep and endure the unbearable for it. The warning that follows is aimed at men, but the trap is described as one for everyone.

notes.quote: 恐るべく慎むべきはこの惑ひなり
notes.text: 自ら{戒|いまし}めて: 'admonish yourself'. Sections 8 and 9 belong together: 8 says nothing leads people astray like lust, 9 says it is the one attachment nobody can give up. It is a Buddhist warning, written by a priest. Compare section 3, where a man with no interest in love is 'a beautiful jade cup with no bottom'. Both views run through the whole book: the old court culture, where knowing love is part of being cultured, and Buddhism, where it is the deepest attachment. The book never settles the question; it says both.
